location: Abdulhai et al. (2026) [c174] row, report line 70; corresponding recommended-paper notes at line 162
claim: Recommended for the core dataset; report-data.json status_by_cid.c174 = core.
problem: The qualifying diversity result compares controls with subgroups defined by actual AI use, not with the randomized AI-access arm. Random assignment to access does not make these use-selected comparisons randomized. The creativity rating is self-reported and cannot supply the missing qualifying outcome. Supported status: context (observational comparisons by actual use, plus AI-versus-human revision evidence in S2). Core inclusion would require an output-based creativity/diversity comparison of the assigned arms.
evidence: creativity-codebook.md sections 3-4 require randomized AI assistance with an eligible output outcome and code design per estimate. forms/c174.json studies[S1].assignment.what_was_assigned says the LLM and LLM-Influenced groups were not randomized arms; S1-O1.measure_detail says no combined AI-access-versus-control estimate is printed, and both recorded contrasts select use subgroups. S1-O5.scored_on_output is false; eligibility.context_class is ai_vs_human. Independently checked C:/Dropbox/Research/ai-lab/literature/creativity/Abdulhai et al (2026) - How LLMs Distort Our Written Language.pdf: p. 4 randomizes access; p. 5 defines LLM-Influenced using self-reported generation of less than 40% of the text, checked against transcripts; pp. 8-9, Figure 4b and section 4.2, compare heavy-use and low-use groups separately with controls. PDF p. 24 asks how creative writers felt. PDF pp. 5-6 describe S2 as automated revisions of archived human drafts, not AI assistance assigned to those writers.

location: Chen et al. (2026) [c249] row, report line 82; recommended-paper note stating that mixed-group output scores satisfy criterion 3
claim: Recommended for the core dataset; report-data.json status_by_cid.c249 = core, with the mixed-group consensus measure treated as a qualifying across_people outcome.
problem: The qualifying consensus score pools independently generated AI descriptions with human descriptions. It therefore does not establish diversity across human participants' outputs, as required by the codebook. Whether a human-output comparison is available remains explicitly unresolved in the form, but is marked as not affecting eligibility. Supported status: needs clarification of criterion 3 before recommending the paper for the core dataset.
evidence: creativity-codebook.md section 3 requires creativity or diversity scored on participants' output, and section 6 specifies that diversity always compares different people. forms/c249.json S1-O1.diversity_detail.notes says the score pools human and AI descriptions and does not isolate diversity across human writers; final.open_items[6] leaves human-only similarity/content estimates to posted data while marking affects_eligibility=false. Independently checked C:/Dropbox/Research/ai-lab/literature/creativity/Chen Liu Hu Li (2026) - AI agents reshape consensus formation in human groups.pdf: p. 7, Methods M1 equations 1-2, computes consensus over all pairs among N=24 players and then averages over every player; p. 16, Game Procedure, explicitly defines these 24 as a mixture of human players and LLM agents who independently submit descriptions. The human-human similarity in Figure 3a is a baseline comparison before convergence (PDF pp. 4 and 14), not the missing human-output treatment contrast. The form identifies the remaining content/attribution scores as other rather than creativity, and its adoption/influence comparisons are human-versus-agent strata within conditions rather than randomized human arms.
